c.tagline: The largest city of Western Sahara, on the edge of the Atlantic Sahara.

taxi.fareNote: Small 'petits taxis' work within the city and are cheap and metered — insist on the meter (compteur) or agree a price first, and expect to share the cab with other riders. Larger white 'grands taxis' cover the airport and longer runs at a negotiated flat rate. There are no ride-hailing apps.

emergency.note: Dial 19 for police and 15 for ambulance/fire; 112 also works from mobiles. French and Arabic are the languages of officialdom.

solo.f: comfortable if dressed modestly; extra caution

hood_landmark.Foum el Oued: Foum el Oued beach Laayoune Morocco

avoid.reason: No specific no-go districts in town, but stay away from political demonstrations and never travel off-road toward the sand berm east of the territory, which is mined.
Photographing police, military or government buildings can draw questioning in this heavily policed disputed territory; petty crime is otherwise low.

hood_desc: The old Spanish-built colonial quarter at the city's heart, with the whitewashed former cathedral of San Francisco de Asis, the grand Place du Mechouar square and the main administrative buildings; the most walkable base for a first visit.
A central residential and commercial district with markets, cafes and mid-range hotels, giving an everyday feel of the city away from the monumental core.
A large, densely built residential district that grew from earlier tent and self-built housing; local and unpolished, with basic shops and little tourism.
A newer administrative and residential area of wide avenues, government offices and modern apartment blocks; quieter and more spread out.

The Atlantic beach suburb roughly 20 km west at the mouth of the Saguia el-Hamra, with a long sandy shoreline, seaside residences, the fishing port and the city's beach hotels; a weekend escape from the desert heat.

water.note: Stick to bottled water in this desert city.

transit.pay: Pay the bus fare in cash to the driver (a few dirhams); petits taxis are metered and cheap. There is no rechargeable transit card.
transit.hours: City buses run roughly from early morning to mid-evening; petits taxis fill the gaps day and night.
transit.note: Laayoune has no metro, tram or rail; getting around means a basic municipal bus network and, above all, the cheap metered petits taxis for hops around town, with grands taxis for the airport and longer desert runs.

bus: Gare Routiere (CTM / Supratours intercity coaches to Agadir, Marrakesh and Dakhla)

transit.m: Petit or grand taxi to the city center (5-10 min; agree the fare first)
Hotel airport transfer offered by several hotels

tip.r: ~5-10% at sit-down restaurants for good service; round up taxi fares and leave a few dirhams for cafe and hotel staff.
